title: Replication & Sensitivity Analysis R Code
text: This page contains the portable R script (Code/replication_analysis.R) used to generate all tables, statistics, and figures in the replication report.

title: Replication & Sensitivity Analysis R Code
text:
Requirements

R (\(\ge 4.1\)) with tidyverse, estimatr, and scales
Input dataset: Data/butler_nickerson_clean.csv

To reproduce all console outputs locally from the project root:
Rscript Code/replication_analysis.R

title: Replication & Sensitivity Analysis R Code
text:
Full Script (Code/replication_analysis.R)

# POLI 100X Replication & Sensitivity Analysis
# Butler & Nickerson (2011): "Can Learning Constituency Opinion Affect How Legislators Vote?"
# Author: Nolan Yumiaco (UC San Diego)

library(tidyverse)
library(estimatr)
options(scipen = 999)

# Resolve data path whether script is run from project root or Code/
data_path <- if (file.exists("Data/butler_nickerson_clean.csv")) {
  "Data/butler_nickerson_clean.csv"
} else if (file.exists("../Data/butler_nickerson_clean.csv")) {
  "../Data/butler_nickerson_clean.csv"
} else {
  stop("Could not locate Data/butler_nickerson_clean.csv")
}

df <- read_csv(data_path, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    low_support = as.numeric(q2full <= median(q2full, na.rm = TRUE)),
    flt = treatment * low_support
  )

# Summary statistics table for primary variables
summary_vars <- c("sb24", "treatment", "low_support", "flt", "rep", "dem_pres_2party")
summary_labels <- c(
  sb24 = "Voted Yes on SB-24 (sb24)",
  treatment = "Treatment Assigned (treatment)",
  low_support = "Low-Support District (low_support)",
  flt = "Interaction: Treatment x Low Support (flt)",
  rep = "Republican Legislator (rep)",
  dem_pres_2party = "District Dem. Presidential Vote Share"
)

summary_stats <- map_dfr(summary_vars, function(v) {
  vals <- df[[v]]
  tibble(
    Variable = summary_labels[[v]],
    N = sum(!is.na(vals)),
    Mean = mean(vals, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(vals, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min = min(vals, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max = max(vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
})

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Core Replication Models (Linear Probability Models with CR2 Cluster SEs)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Model 1: No controls
m1 <- lm_robust(
  sb24 ~ treatment + flt + low_support,
  data = df,
  clusters = match_category
)

# Model 2: Controlling for legislator party and 2004 district presidential vote
m2 <- lm_robust(
  sb24 ~ treatment + flt + low_support + rep + dem_pres_2party,
  data = df,
  clusters = match_category
)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Extension Approach 1: Iterative Leave-One-Matched-Pair-Out Check (M2)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

pairings <- sort(unique(df$match_category))

leave_one_out <- map_dfr(pairings, function(pair_drop) {
  temp_df <- df |>
    filter(match_category != pair_drop)

  mod <- lm_robust(
    sb24 ~ treatment + flt + low_support + rep + dem_pres_2party,
    data = temp_df,
    clusters = match_category
  )

  flt_row <- tidy(mod) |> filter(term == "flt")

  tibble(
    dropped_pair = pair_drop,
    nobs = mod$nobs,
    nclusters = mod$nclusters,
    flt_coef = flt_row$estimate,
    flt_se = flt_row$std.error,
    ci_low = flt_row$conf.low,
    ci_high = flt_row$conf.high,
    p_value = flt_row$p.value
  )
}) |>
  mutate(
    influential_flag = if_else(
      dropped_pair %in% c(21, 32),
      "Top 2 Most Influential (Pairs 21 & 32)",
      "Other Matched Pair"
    )
  )

# Publication-ready leave-one-pair-out plot
baseline_flt <- unname(coef(m2)["flt"])

loo_plot <- ggplot(
  leave_one_out,
  aes(
    x = reorder(factor(dropped_pair), flt_coef),
    y = flt_coef,
    color = influential_flag
  )
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", color = "#64748b", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline_flt, linetype = "dashed", color = "#1e3a8a", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), width = 0, alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Top 2 Most Influential (Pairs 21 & 32)" = "#dc2626",
      "Other Matched Pair" = "#1e3a8a"
    ),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 3,
    y = baseline_flt + 0.025,
    label = sprintf("Full-sample M2 FLT = %.3f", baseline_flt),
    color = "#1e3a8a",
    hjust = 0,
    size = 3.4,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 34.5,
    y = -0.210 + 0.04,
    label = "Drop Pair 32: -0.210",
    color = "#dc2626",
    hjust = 1,
    size = 3.2,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Leave-One-Pair-Out Sensitivity of the Treatment × Low-Support Interaction (FLT)",
    subtitle = "M2 linear probability model with CR2 95% confidence intervals (clustered by matched pair)",
    x = "Dropped Matched Pair (ordered by FLT estimate)",
    y = "Estimated FLT Coefficient (percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11.5) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12.5, color = "#0f172a"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#475569", size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7.5, angle = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

# -------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Extension Approach 2: Drop Both Most Influential Pairs (21 & 32)
# -------------------------------------------------------------------------

drop_influential <- df |>
  filter(!match_category %in% c(21, 32))

m1_drop <- lm_robust(
  sb24 ~ treatment + flt + low_support,
  data = drop_influential,
  clusters = match_category
)

m2_drop <- lm_robust(
  sb24 ~ treatment + flt + low_support + rep + dem_pres_2party,
  data = drop_influential,
  clusters = match_category
)

# Print outputs when run directly from the command line
if (sys.nframe() == 0) {
  cat("\n--- Model 1 (Full Sample, No Controls) ---\n")
  print(summary(m1))
  cat("\n--- Model 2 (Full Sample, With Controls) ---\n")
  print(summary(m2))
  cat("\n--- Leave-One-Pair-Out Summary (FLT) ---\n")
  print(summary(leave_one_out$flt_coef))
  cat("\n--- Model 1 (Dropping Pairs 21 & 32) ---\n")
  print(summary(m1_drop))
  cat("\n--- Model 2 (Dropping Pairs 21 & 32) ---\n")
  print(summary(m2_drop))
}

title: Do Legislators Change Their Votes When They See District Polling?
text:
Executive Summary
This project replicates Butler and Nickerson (2011), who conducted a randomized field experiment in the New Mexico House of Representatives to test whether giving legislators district-level public opinion polling changes how they vote on a proposed tax-rebate spending bill (SB-24). Legislators in the control group largely defaulted to voting yes, even when their constituents opposed the proposal. Legislators who received district polling data in low-support districts were substantially more likely to vote no.
Using linear probability models (lm_robust) with CR2 standard errors clustered by matched pair, our replication recovers results closely aligned with the original study’s probit estimates. To test whether the headline finding is driven by a handful of observations in this small sample (\(N = 67\) voting legislators across \(35\) matched pairs), we extend the analysis with two matched-pair sensitivity checks:

Leave-one-pair-out loop (Approach 1): Dropping one matched pair at a time keeps the treatment × low-support interaction (FLT) negative in every single iteration (-35.4 to -21.0 percentage points).
Omitting the two most influential pairs together (Approach 2): Removing Pairs 21 and 32 attenuates the controlled FLT interaction from -29.3 pp (\(p = 0.053\)) to -16.1 pp (\(p = 0.202\)), showing that while the sign stays negative, the magnitude and statistical precision of the controlled interaction are sensitive to these two pairs.

Omitting Pair 32 alone yields the largest upward shift, moving FLT from −29.3 pp to −21.0 pp (\(p = 0.109\)).

title: Do Legislators Change Their Votes When They See District Polling?
text:
Experimental Design & Data
Butler and Nickerson studied \(70\) New Mexico House legislators organized into \(35\) matched pairs (match_category 1–35) based on party affiliation, re-election timing, and 2004 election vote share prior to the vote on SB-24. Within each pair, one legislator was randomly assigned to treatment (treatment = 1) and the other to control (treatment = 0):

Treatment: On Friday, August 15, 2008, treated legislators received a physical letter on Yale University letterhead reporting district-level polling results from a \(10,690\)-respondent statewide survey, backed up by an email with identical content.
Outcome (sb24): Roll-call vote on SB-24 (1 = voted yes, 0 = voted no). Three legislators in the dataset (match_category 1, 10, and 22, all control-group members) were excused or have missing votes, leaving \(N = 67\) observed votes across \(35\) clusters.
Low-Support Moderator (low_support): Indicator equal to 1 if district support (q2full) was at or below the sample median, and 0 otherwise.
Interaction Term (flt = treatment * low_support): Measures how the estimated treatment effect differs between low-support and high-support districts. In the regression model:

treatment estimates the treatment effect in high-support districts (low_support = 0).
flt estimates the difference in treatment effect between low- and high-support districts.
treatment + flt gives the total estimated treatment effect in low-support districts.

Interpreting the Baseline vs. Controlled Estimates

Minimal effect in high-support districts: In M2, the treatment coefficient is -0.01865 (SE 0.08262, \(p = 0.824\)), indicating essentially no change in voting behavior when treated legislators already represented high-support districts.
Large negative shift in low-support districts: The interaction flt is -0.41877 (\(p = 0.018\)) in M1 and -0.29334 (\(p = 0.053\)) in M2. Combining treatment + flt in M2 implies an estimated -31.2 percentage-point drop in the probability of voting yes on SB-24 when a legislator in a low-support district is shown district polling.
Why controls matter: Adding legislator party (rep = -0.42003, \(p = 0.007\)) and district 2004 Democratic presidential vote share (dem_pres_2party = 0.45068) substantially increases explanatory power (Adjusted \(R^2\) rises from 0.0577 to 0.4004) and reduces the magnitude of flt by roughly 12.5 percentage points compared to the uncontrolled specification.

text:
Matched-Pair Sensitivity Analysis
Because the experiment relies on \(67\) observed votes across \(35\) matched pairs, a small number of pairs could exert heavy leverage on the interaction estimate.

Approach 1: Iterative Leave-One-Pair-Out Check
Across all \(35\) iterations omitting one match_category pair from M2:

Every estimate remains negative, ranging from -0.354 (when dropping Pair 25, \(p = 0.016\)) to -0.210 (when dropping Pair 32, \(p = 0.109\)).
The median leave-one-out FLT coefficient is -0.2935, nearly identical to the full-sample M2 estimate of -0.29334.
Pairs 32 and 21 produce the two largest upward shifts (weakening the negative interaction the most when omitted).

In M1 (no controls), flt moves modestly from -0.41877 to -0.36315 (\(p = 0.041\)), remaining statistically significant at the 5% level.
In M2 (with controls), flt attenuates from -0.29334 (\(p = 0.053\)) to -0.16119 (\(p = 0.202\)), while treatment shifts from -0.01865 to -0.07048.

This demonstrates an important nuance for interpreting small-\(N\) field experiments: the directional conclusion (polling reduces yes votes in low-support districts) holds across every single-pair deletion and even under joint deletion of the two most influential pairs, but the statistical significance and magnitude of the controlled interaction rely noticeably on Pairs 21 and 32.

title: Do Legislators Change Their Votes When They See District Polling?
text:
Limitations & Methodological Notes

Sample size and statistical power: Dropping two pairs removes 4 of 70 legislators (leaving \(N = 63\) observed votes). Removing the two pairs most supportive of the hypothesis naturally reduces precision and does not prove a null effect, but it highlights how sensitive small-sample interaction estimates can be.
External validity: The experiment tested one straightforward fiscal bill (tax rebate SB-24) in a single state legislature (New Mexico). Legislators may respond differently on salient, partisan, or socially controversial issues.
Non-compliance / trustee behavior: Receiving a letter or email does not guarantee a legislator read it or chose to act as a delegate rather than a trustee.
Reconciliation note vs. original class PDF: All tables, statistics, and plots on this page are rendered dynamically from Code/replication_analysis.R. Compared to the original class PDF report, this web edition preserves the exact coefficient estimates while correcting minor transcription typos in the PDF tables (specifically: Full M2 Clusters = 35 instead of 45; and the Drop-21-&-32 table title "Drop Pairs 21 and 32" instead of "31 and 52", with N = 63, Clusters = 33, and M2 Adjusted $R^2 = 0.4869`).
